title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: last — foresight election overturns pure grace
latin: Ultimum argumentum nostrum hujusmodi erit: Non debemus introducere talem electionem, quae puram Dei gratiam evertit, et discrimen electorum et rejectorum ad bonum usum liberi arbitrii reducit: Sed electio ex fide praevisa, et non-electio ex infidelitate praevisa hoc facit.
pass_a: Our last argument will be of this kind: We ought not to introduce such an election as overturns the pure grace of God, and reduces the discrimination of elect and rejected to the good use of free choice: But election from foresighted faith, and non-election from foresighted unbelief, does this.
pass_b: Last argument: we must not bring in an election that overturns pure grace and reduces the split between elect and rejected to the good use of free choice. But election from foresighted faith — and non-election from foresighted unbelief — does exactly that.

lemmas.gloss: reduces the discrimen to free choice's good use

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: major — Augustine: true grace needs absolute predestination (De bono persever. 2)
latin: Ad Majorem quod attinet, tam clara est, ut pudeat ipsos adversarios aperte asserere hanc specialem electionis gratiam aliunde, quam ex mero et solo Dei beneplacito dependere. At sapienter hoc expendit Augustinus, non posse talem gratuitam gratiam stabiliri, nisi stabiliatur simul absoluta haec praedestinatio, et minime ex praeviis arbitrii humani operationibus suspensa, De bono persever. cap. 2. Praedestinatio, inquit, praedicenda est, ut possit vera Dei gratia, hoc est, quae non secundum merita nostra detur, insuperabili munitione defendi. Praedestinationem autem intelligit, non Arminianam ex praevisione fidei et perseverantiae humanae ortam, sed Paulinam, quae fidem et perseverantiam electis praeparat ab aeterno, donatque tempore opportuno. Sine hac igitur praedestinatione, quam toto illo libro propugnat Augustinus, judicavit veram Dei gratiam non posse defendi.
pass_a: As to the Major, it is so clear that the adversaries themselves are ashamed openly to assert that this special grace of election depends from elsewhere than from the mere and sole good pleasure of God. But wisely Augustine weighs this, that such gratuitous grace cannot be established, unless at the same time this absolute predestination be established, and by no means suspended from the previous operations of human choice, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 2. Predestination, he says, is to be preached, that true grace of God, that is, which is not given according to our merits, may be able to be defended by an impregnable fortification. But he understands predestination, not the Arminian arisen from foresight of human faith and perseverance, but the Pauline, which prepares faith and perseverance for the elect from eternity, and gives them in due time. Without this predestination therefore, which Augustine defends through that whole book, he judged that the true grace of God cannot be defended.
pass_b: The major is so clear adversaries are ashamed to say outright that this special election-grace hangs on anything but God's mere sole good pleasure. Augustine wisely weighs it (On the Gift of Perseverance 2): such free grace cannot stand unless absolute predestination stands with it — not hung on prior acts of human choice. Predestination must be preached, he says, so true grace (not given according to our merits) can be defended by impregnable walls. He means not Arminian predestination from foresight of human faith and perseverance, but Pauline — which prepares faith and perseverance for the elect from eternity and gives them in due time. Without that predestination, which Augustine defends through the whole book, he judged true grace cannot be defended.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: sounder scholastics — willing to receive grace is from predestination
latin: Quinetiam ipsi Scholastici saniores, qui plus aequo tribuere solent humano arbitrio, tamen non audent electorum et praeteritorum discrimen ad bonum et malum usum liberi arbitrii in gratia amplexanda vel repellenda revocare. Unde Thomas, Qu. disp. de praed. art. 2: Hoc ipsum velle accipere gratiam est ex praedestinatione Divina. Et Durandus, pag. 250: Omne bonum quod fit ab aliquo, vel quod juvat eum ad consecutionem finis supernaturalis, sive per causam, sive per occasionem, cadit sub effectu praedestinationis.
pass_a: Moreover the sounder Scholastics themselves, who are wont to attribute more than is equal to human choice, yet do not dare to recall the discrimination of elect and passed-by to the good and bad use of free choice in embracing or rejecting grace. Whence Thomas, Disputed Questions on Predestination, article 2: This very willing to receive grace is from Divine predestination. And Durandus, p. 250: Every good that is done by someone, or that helps him to the attainment of the supernatural end, whether by cause or by occasion, falls under the effect of predestination.
pass_b: Even the sounder scholastics, who usually credit free choice more than is due, dare not reduce the split between elect and passed-by to good or bad use of free choice in embracing or rejecting grace. So Aquinas (Disputed Questions on Predestination, art. 2): this very willing to receive grace is from divine predestination. And Durandus (p. 250): every good done by someone, or that helps him reach the supernatural end — whether as cause or occasion — falls under predestination's effect.

lemmas.gloss: willing to receive grace is from predestination
every helping good falls under predestination's effect

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: minor first — eternal favor given or denied by prior free-choice use
latin: Jam ad Minorem accedamus. Dicimus ergo hanc electionem et praeteritionem, quam ex fide et infidelitate praevisa fieri defendunt, gratiam Dei ex merito humanae voluntatis suspendere. Primo igitur: Gratia Dei propriissime sumpta est favor ille, vel aeterna Dei benevolentia secundum quam vult huic singulari personae vitam aeternam conferre. At hic amor sive favor Dei, quod est primum donum in quo caetera omnia donantur, ex sententia Remonstrantium datur et negatur prout homines prius bene aut male usi fuerint libero suo arbitrio, in admittenda aut repellenda illa sufficienti gratia quam omnibus oblatam asseverant. Hoc perinde est, ac si dicerent, Deus hominem ad vitam aeternam amare incepit, quia hominis liberum arbitrium ad gratiam se applicavit.
pass_a: Now let us come to the Minor. We say therefore that this election and passing by, which they defend as done from foresighted faith and unbelief, suspends the grace of God from the merit of the human will. First therefore: The grace of God taken most properly is that favor, or eternal benevolence of God according to which he wills to confer eternal life on this singular person. But this love or favor of God, which is the first gift in which all the rest are given, according to the Remonstrants' opinion is given and denied according as men shall first have used their free choice well or ill, in admitting or rejecting that sufficient grace which they affirm offered to all. This is just as if they said, God began to love a man unto eternal life, because the man's free choice applied itself to grace.
pass_b: Now the minor. This election and passing by from foresighted faith and unbelief, we say, hangs God's grace on the merit of the human will. First: grace of God most properly is that favor — eternal benevolence — by which he wills to confer eternal life on this singular person. But that love or favor, the first gift in which all others are given, the Remonstrants have given or denied as men first used free choice well or ill in admitting or rejecting the sufficient grace they say is offered to all. That is as much as to say: God began to love a man unto eternal life because the man's free choice applied itself to grace.

lemmas.gloss: grace as eternal favor to a singular person

lemmas.lemma: liberum arbitrium ad gratiam se applicavit
lemmas.gloss: God's love begins because free choice applied itself

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: minor second — why faith in Peter not Judas? special free-choice act
latin: Secundo, Gratia Dei dicuntur illa dona supernaturalia, quibus Spiritus sanctus imbuit, refingit et vivificat animas nostras, qualia sunt fides, charitas, reliquaque quibus omnes regenerati donantur. Haec etiam gratia juxta opinionem Arminii datur aut non datur pro diversis meritis humanarum voluntatum. Nam si electio ex fide praevisa consequatur, quaero unde haec fides in Petro potius quam in Juda fuerit praevisa. Non possunt obtendere specialem gratiam in praedestinatione Petro praeparatam causam fuisse quod is crediderit; quia hanc praedestinationem explodunt, et fidem praedestinatione priorem statuunt. Recurrant itaque necesse est ad specialem actum liberi arbitrii, in Petro specialiter sese accommodantis ad illa media, quae Deus ad fidem generandam non minus Judae quam Petro suppeditavit. At hoc quid aliud est, quam agnoscere gratiam monitricem, aut motricem humanae voluntatis ex mera Dei misericordia omnibus promiscue offerri, sed gratiam voluntatis vivificatricem pro diversis singulorum meritis in illa priore gratia accipienda aut repellenda conferri.
pass_a: Secondly, by the grace of God are meant those supernatural gifts with which the Holy Spirit imbues, reshapes, and vivifies our souls, such as are faith, charity, and the rest with which all the regenerate are gifted. This grace also according to Arminius's opinion is given or not given according to the diverse merits of human wills. For if election follows from foresighted faith, I ask whence this faith was foresighted in Peter rather than in Judas. They cannot pretend that special grace prepared for Peter in predestination was the cause that he believed; because they explode this predestination, and set faith prior to predestination. They must therefore recur to a special act of free choice, in Peter specially accommodating itself to those means which God supplied no less to Judas than to Peter for generating faith. But what else is this, than to acknowledge that admonishing or moving grace of the human will is offered from the mere mercy of God promiscuously to all, but that vivifying grace of the will is conferred according to the diverse merits of individuals in accepting or rejecting that prior grace.
pass_b: Second: grace of God also means those supernatural gifts by which the Holy Spirit imbues, reshapes, and vivifies our souls — faith, charity, and the rest given to all the regenerate. On Arminius's view that grace too is given or withheld by the diverse merits of human wills. If election follows foresighted faith, why was that faith foresighted in Peter rather than Judas? They cannot claim special grace prepared for Peter in predestination caused him to believe — they explode that predestination and set faith prior to it. So they must fall back on a special free-choice act in Peter, specially fitting itself to means God supplied no less to Judas than to Peter for generating faith. What is that but to grant that admonishing or moving grace is offered from mere mercy to all alike, while vivifying grace of the will is conferred by each one's diverse merits in accepting or rejecting that prior grace?

lemmas.lemma: unde haec fides in Petro potius quam in Juda
lemmas.gloss: why foresight faith in Peter not Judas
vivifying grace by merits in accepting prior grace

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13: Pelagius's grace vs Augustine's — Miserebor cuius misertus fuero
latin: Scio Arminii discipulos hoc negare: sed velint nolint, stabilita hac praedestinatione hominum ex praevisione fidei, non possunt aliam gratiam admittere, quam eam quam tandem admisit ipse Pelagius; non possunt illam agnoscere, quam ubique ut fateatur, urget Augustinus. Sed qualem gratiam admisit Pelagius? Operatur Deus in nobis velle quod bonum est, velle quod sanctum est, dum nos terrenis cupiditatibus deditos futurae gloriae magnitudine et praemiorum pollicitatione succendit, dum revelatione sapientiae in desiderium Dei stupentem suscitat voluntatem, dum nobis suadet omne quod bonum est. Haec profecto sunt ea media quibus administratis Arminius fingit Deum speculari quinam credituri sunt, quinam non credituri, et sic eos ad vitam eligere, quos praevidet recte iis usuros, eos praeterire quos praevidet iisdem abusuros. Sed quid ad hoc Augustinus? Nos, inquit, eam gratiam nolumus. Istam fateatur Pelagius, qua futurae gloriae magnitudo non solum promittitur, verum etiam creditur et speratur; nec solum revelatur sapientia, verum etiam et amatur; nec suadetur solum omne quod bonum est, verum et persuadetur. Hanc autem gratiam quae fidem, spem et charitatem infundit, quae facit ut faciamus, ea est quam non ex merito dari contendebant Catholici, hoc est, non ex praeeunte bono usu liberi arbitrii, sed ex mera misericordia Dei. Sic in Concilio Diospolitano praecipitur Pelagio, ut fateatur gratiam Dei non dari secundum merita nostra: atque haec ratio subjungitur, Ut vera sit gratia, id est, gratis data per ejus misericordiam qui dixit, MISEREBOR CUIUS MISERTUS FUERO.
pass_a: I know Arminius's disciples deny this: but whether they will or nill, this predestination of men from foresight of faith being established, they cannot admit another grace than that which at last Pelagius himself admitted; they cannot acknowledge that which Augustine everywhere urges that he confess. But what kind of grace did Pelagius admit? God works in us to will what is good, to will what is holy, while he kindles us given over to earthly desires by the greatness of future glory and the promise of rewards, while by revelation of wisdom he raises the astonished will into desire of God, while he persuades us of everything that is good. These indeed are those means by whose administration Arminius feigns that God watches who will believe, who will not believe, and so elects to life those whom he foresees will use them rightly, and passes by those whom he foresees will abuse the same. But what says Augustine to this? We, he says, do not will that grace. Let Pelagius confess that, by which the greatness of future glory is not only promised, but also believed and hoped; nor is wisdom only revealed, but also loved; nor is everything good only advised, but also persuaded. But this grace which infuses faith, hope, and charity, which makes us that we may do, is that which the Catholics contended is not given from merit, that is, not from a preceding good use of free choice, but from the mere mercy of God. So in the Council of Diospolis it is enjoined on Pelagius that he confess the grace of God is not given according to our merits: and this reason is subjoined, That it may be true grace, that is, freely given through the mercy of him who said, I WILL HAVE MERCY ON WHOM I WILL HAVE MERCY.
pass_b: Arminius's disciples deny it — but will they or nill they, once predestination from foresight of faith is fixed, they can admit no grace but what Pelagius at last admitted; they cannot own what Augustine everywhere presses him to confess. What grace did Pelagius grant? God works in us to will the good and the holy while he kindles us by future glory and promised rewards, raises the stunned will by wisdom's revelation into desire of God, and advises us of every good. Those are the very means by whose administration Arminius has God watching who will believe and who will not — electing those he foresees will use them well, passing by those he foresees will abuse them. Augustine: We do not want that grace. Let Pelagius confess the grace by which future glory is not only promised but believed and hoped; wisdom not only revealed but loved; every good not only advised but persuaded. That grace which pours in faith, hope, and charity, and makes us do — Catholics held it is not given from merit, not from prior good use of free choice, but from God's mere mercy. So at Diospolis Pelagius is ordered to confess grace is not given according to our merits — reason: that it may be true grace, freely given through the mercy of him who said, I WILL HAVE MERCY ON WHOM I WILL HAVE MERCY.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 13 close: two impieties — explode foresight election; good use is benefit, not mover
latin: Ut verbo absolvam: Quandoquidem haec opinio de electione singularium personarum ad vitam ex praevisa fide eorundem involvit haec duo maxime gratiae inimica, nempe, Primum Dei amorem quo ad vitam destinat singulares personas oriri ex bono usu liberi arbitrii per gratiam praeventi, et ipsam fidem non certis personis ex speciali dono infundi, sed ex speciali bono actu liberi arbitrii in certis personis concipi, ab omnibus orthodoxis explodenda est; et e contra statuendum, bonum usum gratiae a Deo praescitum non fuisse causam quae Deum movebat ut hos prae aliis eligeret, sed fuisse potius speciale beneficium electionis.
pass_a: To finish in a word: Since this opinion of the election of singular persons to life from their foresighted faith involves these two things most hostile to grace, namely, that the first love of God by which he destines singular persons to life arises from the good use of free choice prevented by grace, and that faith itself is not infused into certain persons from a special gift, but is conceived in certain persons from a special good act of free choice, it is to be exploded by all the orthodox; and on the contrary it is to be established that the good use of grace foreknown by God was not the cause which moved God to elect these before others, but was rather a special benefit of election.
pass_b: In a word: this view — electing singular persons to life from their foresighted faith — involves two things most hostile to grace: that God's first love destining them to life arises from the good use of grace-prevented free choice; and that faith itself is not infused into certain persons by a special gift, but conceived in them by a special good act of free choice. All the orthodox must explode it. On the contrary: the good use of grace God foreknew was not the cause that moved him to elect these before others — it was rather a special benefit of election.

lemmas.gloss: two things most hostile to grace
good use is benefit of election, not its mover
